title: Creole dancing, costumes and real Indians of her youth
summary: She describes Creole dances and Indian dress, and real Indians who stayed at her grandmother's and sold at the Indian market.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs

blocks.x: You're not missing much. What was it like in the old days?

Oh, they'd sing all them songs that you're asking me about. They'd sing, they'd dance, the dance of the, you know, Creole dance. And they'd skip. And they'd dress like, well, if there was a bunch of Indians, well, then they would dress like Indians. Now they don't dress like Indians. They would dress like real Indians, with them blue dress and a yellow strip, you know, bias on the dress. Oh, yes. A little short waist. And the hair just tied, what they call it, pony now, pony. Pony tail. Pony tail. Yeah. Well, that's the way the Indians, the real Indians used to just have their hair tied like that.
Well, did any of the songs they sang come from Haiti or San Domingo?
Well, I don't, yes, I guess so.

Do you remember the names of any of the songs which came from Haiti or San Domingo, the Indians sang? I think some of the Creole songs undoubtedly came from Haiti. Yes. Because that's the language they speak, you know, Creole, it's Creole.

A while ago, Dave, before you came, we were speaking about the Indians and how they dressed. Yeah. And I was telling them children when I was in my teens that I would go to ball because we didn't, girls didn't run around like they do now. It was a pleasure then to look at the Indians. They were dressed like real Indians. They had that basket on the back, you know, and they sat on the floor and they'd eat the cowpies. I believe it was jambalaya. Jambalaya congri. It sat on the floor. But now the Indians, they've got all kinds of stones and things on the, not Indian enough.
You want a Coke or anything? Yes, I like a Coke. You want a Coke? Yes. All right, if you have something. Maybe I'll take that instead of a Coke. I don't know. I don't drink that.
You know how they call that? In Creole, peep. Peep. Peep.
Peep, yeah. Uh, what about the Indians? Did you hear any real Indians sing, Yabba?
The real Indians that were here.
Oh, I don't know. They didn't, the real Indians didn't bother. You know, real Indians, they don't talk much. Oui, no. Ma palais. But, uh, they didn't bother about Mardi Gras and things like that.
Well, where did you see the real Indians in those days?

At my grandmother's. When I was a child, she always had Indians that would come from Bafouca and I don't know where across the lake there. And she, when they'd come, they used to be at that market they called Lahal Sovar, Indian market. It's Bayou Road on the other side of the road. No, on this side of the road. And when they was too far from my grandmother, they'd sleep in the, in the yard inside the, what's the name? But when they was closer to my, my grandmother's place, they would come home. Sometimes there'd be three, four of them. And she'd just leave them lay asleep there. And give them coffee. They had one they called Catherine. And she'd give them coffee in the morning. They, Catherine, to Paulie, coffee. Oui. She'd give them coffee. The minute they take the left, the last drop, ma palais. They'd tell her, I'm going. Yes, I saw some real Indians.
